channel.title: MIA — Management Intelligence Alert
channel.description: daily selected and enriched macroeconomic and political news

item.title: Europe's drought deepened into an economic drag: the Rhine fell to a record-low six centimetres at Kaub, hitting freight, and French sugar-beet and Comté-cheese output collapsed, while floods forced relief in Pakistan and India.
item.description:
The slow-building climate shock reported in recent alerts hardened into concrete damage. Germany's rivers are at record lows: the Rhine — a key artery for bulk chemicals and raw materials — is now effectively divided into stretches north and south of Kaub, where the gauge hit just six centimetres, the lowest since detailed records began, forcing shippers to sail part-loaded or reroute. In France, the Cristal Union sugar group flagged beet-yield losses of 20–30% as plants died of thirst and pests spread, Comté cheese producers reported sharp milk losses ("losing a Comté a day"), and supermarkets agreed to relax cosmetic standards on drought-hit fruit and vegetables. In Japan, extreme heat is pushing an ageing farm workforce to work at night, with heat-related farm deaths at record levels. In South Asia the mirror problem struck: Pakistan grappled with a "water paradox" of floods and scarcity, and India's Odisha state announced INR 10 billion in flood relief.

Industry Impact

Low water on the Rhine is a direct and recurring constraint on moving bulk chemicals, resins and raw materials through Europe's industrial heartland, raising freight costs and lead times and, at extremes, forcing production curbs at riverside plants. Crop failures feed through to bio-based feedstocks and to food-and-beverage customers whose demand drives packaging adhesives and coatings, while higher food prices add to the inflation the central banks are already fighting. The pattern — European drought and Asian floods in the same week — underlines that climate disruption is now a standing supply-chain and cost variable for the chemical and ACS industry, to be planned for rather than treated as exceptional.

Handelsblatt | Reussir | Le Parisien | Lianhe Zaobao | New Indian Express

item.title: Russia kept earning billions from energy sales to Europe despite 21 EU sanction packages — EU imports of Russian LNG hit a record in early 2026 — as Poland scrambled jets against Russian strikes on Ukraine and the war's political fallout widened.
item.description:
The limits of sanctions came into focus. Despite 21 EU packages, Russia still earns billions from energy exports to Europe, and measures against its banks show little effect; EU imports of Russian liquefied natural gas even reached a record high in the first quarter, up 16% year-on-year (IEEFA data), leaving Russia the EU's second-largest LNG supplier after the US. The fighting pressed on: Poland activated military aircraft and put air-defence and radar systems on heightened alert as Russia launched long-range strikes on Ukraine, a preventive move to secure NATO airspace. The war's politics widened too — Ukraine's dismissed former defence minister Mykhailo Fedorov called for a wartime presidential election, the sharpest internal challenge yet to President Zelensky, while the UN condemned Moscow's exclusion of the anti-war Yabloko party from September's elections and the eleven-year sentence handed to one of its deputies. Moscow, for its part, touted 12.5% first-half industrial growth in its capital.

Industry Impact

For manufacturers the practical message is that Europe's energy-security premium and the Russia-linked risk backdrop are durable, not fading — sanctions have not cut the revenue funding the war, and continued dependence on Russian LNG keeps European gas and power prices exposed to political shocks. That matters directly to energy-intensive chemical production. Heightened NATO-border military activity and widening political instability in both Ukraine and Russia add a standing layer of logistics and country risk to any supply chain touching the region, reinforcing the case for diversified energy and raw-material sourcing.

Wirtschafts Woche | Anadolu Agency | Chinatimes.com | Frankfurter Rundschau

item.title: US agencies warned of an "active threat" to Siemens control systems running water and other critical plants, amid suspected Iran-linked attacks, as a survey found 30% of manufacturers hit by cyber incidents and reshoring increasingly hinges on AI.
item.description:
The physical and digital risks of the moment converged on the factory floor. US cybersecurity agencies issued an advisory describing an "active threat" to all Siemens S7-series programmable logic controllers — the industrial computers that operate water utilities and other critical infrastructure — amid a wave of intrusions into local water systems that experts suspect are tied to Iran, linking the Middle East conflict to industrial-control cyber risk. A Make UK report found 30% of manufacturers suffered a cyber incident, directly or through their supply chain, in the past year, calling cybersecurity an "operational risk" that travels downstream through interconnected suppliers. On the productivity side, a survey found 88% of manufacturing executives say their reshoring plans depend materially on AI-enabled operations, and 74% say at least one reshoring case would fail without AI. China, meanwhile, reported its AI-related industry topped CNY 1 trillion in 2025 with growth above 30%, scaling applications across production and services.

Industry Impact

Chemical and ACS plants run on the same Siemens-class controllers now flagged as targets, so the advisory is a direct prompt to patch, segment operational-technology networks and rehearse incident response — a production-continuity and safety issue, not just IT. The Make UK finding that attacks spread through supply chains means a supplier's breach can halt a customer's line, raising the bar on vendor security due diligence. At the same time, the reshoring-needs-AI data confirm that automation and analytics are now the precondition for bringing production back to high-cost countries — the same logic driving the robotics build-out elsewhere in this alert.

The Economic Times | Valor Econômico | Supply Chain Digital | AP News | China Economic Net

item.title: India pressed its domestic build-out: the cabinet approved INR 130.41 billion of rail and highway projects, real estate drew USD 3.5–4 billion and stayed resilient to the oil shock, and the state moved to seed a market for home-designed chips.
item.description:
Even as growth forecasts were trimmed on oil and weather risk, India kept investing in capacity. The Union Cabinet cleared five infrastructure projects worth INR 130.41 billion — a four-lane highway in Bihar plus four railway multi-tracking schemes adding about 410 km of track across four eastern states to ease freight and passenger corridors. Property held up: capital inflows into real estate reached USD 3.5–4 billion in the first half, and ratings agency CareEdge judged the sector resilient to the West Asia (Middle East) crisis on strong developer balance sheets and office leasing, though a prolonged oil spike could raise construction costs 2–3% and squeeze affordable housing. New Delhi also moved to use public procurement and security rules to create a guaranteed market for India-designed semiconductor chips, warehousing capacity boomed on quick-commerce demand, and Escorts Kubota broke ground on a INR 20 billion equipment plant near Jewar airport.

Industry Impact

India remains one of the strongest structural demand stories for adhesives, coatings and sealants, anchored in infrastructure, construction, autos and a fast-widening electronics base. The INR 130 billion of rail and road work feeds directly into demand for construction chemicals, protective coatings and sealants, while resilient real estate sustains the decorative and building-products segments. New chip and equipment plants add specialty-chemical and materials demand. The watch-item is imported oil inflation, which lifts feedstock and construction costs and could pressure margins in price-sensitive segments — but the investment pipeline keeps India's medium-term ACS trajectory intact.

The Times of India | New Indian Express | Business Standard | LiveMint | New Indian Express

item.title: Southeast Asia stayed resilient: Indonesia grew 5.29% in the second quarter and held rates at 5.75%, Thailand's output and factory sentiment improved, but foreign inflows into Asian bonds fell to a four-month low as the oil shock bit.
item.description:
The region kept outperforming a shaky global backdrop. Indonesia's GDP rose 5.29% year-on-year in the second quarter (5.45% for the first half), helped by fiscal stimulus, and the government is preparing "new growth engines" — downstream processing of coal, copper and other minerals — to chase an 8% target; Bank Indonesia held its policy rate at 5.75%, judging it right for stability amid Middle East–driven oil-price risk. Thailand's economy grew 1.9% in the second quarter, and its industrial sentiment index rose for a second straight month on strong EV sales and government support, with exports on track for double-digit growth. The main caution sign was in capital flows: foreign investment into the local-currency bond markets of India, Indonesia, Malaysia, South Korea and Thailand fell to USD 2.03 billion in July, the smallest since March, as investors turned selective on the conflict and higher oil prices.

Industry Impact

Southeast Asia is one of the more reliable demand stories for adhesives, coatings and sealants, tied to resilient construction, autos, electronics and packaged consumer goods, plus a growing manufacturing base as supply chains diversify out of China. Indonesia's minerals-downstreaming push and Thailand's EV strength create specific openings for industrial and specialty ACS inputs. The cooling bond inflows are a reminder that a prolonged oil shock could tighten financing and currencies across the region, raising import costs for chemical inputs and testing the resilience — so suppliers should treat the growth as solid but sensitive to energy prices.

Antara News | Antara News | The Nation | Bangkok Post | The Economic Times

item.title: China's carmakers pressed abroad and upmarket: Chinese-brand sales in Indonesia jumped 82% in seven months, a wave of gadget-laden EVs targeted younger buyers, and the sector's "founding father" said it had entered a new stage.
item.description:
The industry's outward and upward drive was visible across markets. In Indonesia, 94,971 Chinese-branded vehicles sold in January–July, up 82% year-on-year, as Chinese makers deepened dealer and after-sales networks; in Australia, battery-electric vehicles reached 21.7% of July sales with Chinese brands expanding fast. At home, a new wave of EVs packed with karaoke systems, projector headlights, voice AI assistants and VR cockpits is being launched to win younger drivers — a shift from price wars toward experience and features. Wan Gang, the "founding father" of China's new-energy-vehicle (NEV) industry, said the sector has entered a "new development stage": annual output rose from about 26 million vehicles in 2021 to 34 million in 2025, led by NEVs, and he argued overcapacity should be judged by demand, not volume alone. The globalisation even loops back to the West — Waymo imports Geely Zeekr vehicles for its US robotaxi fleet, paying over 125% in tariffs.

Industry Impact

Autos are a core end-market for adhesives, coatings, sealants and structural bonding, and the centre of gravity is moving toward Chinese OEMs and their overseas plants. Chinese-brand growth in Indonesia, Australia and beyond creates fresh local demand for automotive ACS inputs — an opportunity for suppliers with regional footprints — while the feature-rich, electrified product mix raises the value of specialty adhesives for batteries, displays and lightweight assembly. The flip side is intensifying competition and pricing pressure as Chinese capacity scales, and tariff walls (as Waymo's 125% bill shows) that keep reshaping where vehicles and their inputs can profitably flow.

Xinhua | South China Morning Post | Commercial Times | People's Daily | Forbes

item.title: China's youth unemployment jumped to an 11-month high of 17.9% in July as a record graduate wave met a soft economy, and Beijing answered with an 18-point plan to lift consumption in smaller cities and a drive to grow "future industries".
item.description:
The demand-side weakness behind China's stimulus push showed clearly in the labour data. Urban unemployment for 16–24-year-olds (excluding students) rose to 17.9% in July from 14.9% in June — the highest since September 2025 — as a record cohort of graduates entered a job market strained by the property slump and cautious private hiring; the 25–29 rate edged up to 7.2%. In response, the Ministry of Commerce and eight other departments issued an 18-measure guideline to energise "lower-tier" county and small-city markets by upgrading retail, courting brand debut stores, promoting trade-ins and expanding rural e-commerce and services. Beijing also leaned on longer-term growth engines: President Xi called developing "future industries" a way to seize the commanding heights of technology, "new drivers" contributed 50.9% of industrial growth in the first seven months, high-tech output rose 16.9% in July, and an ageing population is spawning a fast-growing "silver economy" of care and rehabilitation robots.

Industry Impact

Stronger county-level consumption and trade-in schemes would support demand for appliances, vehicles, home improvement and construction in China's interior — all end-markets for adhesives, coatings and sealants. But high youth unemployment is a warning that household confidence is fragile, capping how fast that demand can recover while property stays weak. The pivot toward "future industries", high-tech manufacturing and the silver economy shows where Chinese demand growth is being steered — automation, electronics, healthcare devices — and therefore where specialty ACS producers should aim, rather than at the saturated, price-competitive mass segments.

Lianhe Zaobao | Business Standard | China Daily | Xhby.net | China Daily

item.title: Fed minutes showed policymakers held rates at 3.50–3.75% but split three ways over inflation and saw a hike as possible, even as Trump demanded cuts and the 30-year Treasury yield hit its highest since 2007.
item.description:
The record of the 28–29 July meeting showed the US central bank holding its benchmark rate at 3.50–3.75% in a 9–3 vote — the first time since 2016 that three officials dissented in the same direction, all favouring a quarter-point hike. Many policymakers said higher rates would be needed unless inflation, which has overshot the 2% target for five years, makes more progress; fresh pressure is coming from the Iran war and AI-linked investment. Hours later President Trump publicly urged the Fed to cut rates at its next meeting, saying it is "so afraid of inflation". The tension played out in bond markets: the 30-year Treasury yield reached 5.34%, the highest since 2007, and the 10-year hit 4.75%, on worries about government deficits, sticky inflation and slow rate rises elsewhere (notably the Bank of Japan). A Boston Fed study offered some comfort, finding strong US productivity had blunted tariffs' inflation hit, adding only about 0.5 point to core prices.

Industry Impact

Higher-for-longer US rates and 2007-high long-term yields raise the cost of capital for the construction, housing and industrial projects that consume adhesives, coatings and sealants, and lift borrowing costs for chemical producers' own investment. A politicised Fed adds uncertainty to the dollar and to global financing conditions that emerging-market customers depend on. The one bright spot — productivity absorbing tariff costs — helps explain why US demand has held up despite the trade shock, but the direction of travel is dearer money and a higher hurdle for demand-sensitive, capital-intensive projects.

The New York Times | The Economic Times | Anadolu Agency | Yahoo Finance

item.title: ECB chief Lagarde warned Europe's post-war growth model is "eroding" as the IMF put US output at USD 32.4 trillion against the EU's 23 trillion and a quarter of German industrial firms reported losing competitiveness abroad.
item.description:
A cluster of signals pointed to a structural competitiveness problem, not just a soft patch. Christine Lagarde said Europe's model — built on expanding global trade, a US-backed security order and strength in mid-tech manufacturing — is being undermined as protectionism spreads (over 2,500 new trade restrictions worldwide in ten months of 2025) and as China now competes directly in close to 40% of the sectors the euro area relies on. She warned Europe "cannot afford" to miss the AI revolution, but that fragmented national markets and weak financing stop firms scaling up. The scale of the drift is stark: the IMF projects 2026 US GDP at USD 32.4 trillion versus USD 23 trillion for the 27 EU states — the bloc now just 71% of the US economy, having been larger at the century's start. On the ground, a Munich Ifo survey found 25.4% of German industrial firms see worsening competitiveness outside the EU (43% in autos), and the VDMA engineering lobby said Germany and Europe "need more determination and more speed" to turn research into scaled production.

Industry Impact

For a European-headquartered chemicals and ACS industry this is the strategic backdrop to everything else in this alert: softer domestic industrial demand, tougher Chinese competition, and pressure to justify European production against cheaper locations. It strengthens the case for the deregulation and speed the sector has lobbied for, and makes AI-driven productivity and scale — not incremental cost-cutting — the differentiator. Expect the "competitiveness" argument to shape looming EU decisions on energy prices, chemicals regulation and state aid, all of which bear directly on where ACS capacity is built and kept.

Anadolu Agency | Asharq Al-Awsat | Vedomosti | Wirtschafts Woche | VDMA

item.title: Unitree's Shanghai debut soared about 460%, valuing the humanoid-robot maker near CNY 342 billion as China's robot-industry revenue rose 24.5%, prompting Germany's engineering lobby to urge Europe to build its own robot supply chains.
item.description:
The listing flagged in recent alerts delivered a spectacular first day. Unitree Robotics opened up 629% and closed 460% above its issue price on Shanghai's STAR tech board, reaching a market value near CNY 342 billion (about EUR 7.8 billion) — the first pure humanoid-robot stock on China's A-share market. It debuted alongside the 2026 World Robot Conference in Beijing, where more than 300 firms showed over 2,000 products and the industry ministry pledged support; the head of the US automation association A3 said China now leads the global robotics race, backed by national strategy and scale, while the US still has none. China's above-scale robot makers grew revenue 24.5% year-on-year to CNY 165.5 billion in the first half, and domestic investors have poured over CNY 100 billion into humanoids this year. The surge prompted a pointed European response: Germany's VDMA engineering association urged Europe to put humanoid robotics "at the top of the political agenda" and build resilient domestic supply chains for critical parts, warning that Chinese makers dominate a global humanoid market that nearly quadrupled to 19,100 units in the first half.

Industry Impact

China's robotics scale cuts two ways for Western manufacturers. Cheaper, more capable robots lower the cost of automating mixing, filling, packaging and inspection in adhesives, coatings and sealants plants — a productivity opportunity. But the same build-out entrenches a formidable Chinese supplier base and, via firms expanding into Europe, a new competitor on home turf. The VDMA's alarm signals a coming European industrial-policy push on robotics and critical-component sovereignty that could bring subsidies and local-content preferences. For ACS producers the practical read is to plan automation around a fast-falling cost curve while watching where robot supply chains — and their dependencies — are being anchored.

China Economic Net | Cinco Días | MarketScreener | Global Times | China Economic Net

item.title: Europe's chemical rulebook pulled two ways: Germany missed the EU industrial-emissions deadline and faces a possible EU-wide "carcinogen" label on talc used in coatings, while the UK added a carbon border tax and China renewed anti-dumping duties.
item.description:
For the Adhesives, Coatings & Sealants (ACS) chain the compliance picture grew more tangled rather than simply tighter. Germany missed the 1 July deadline to transpose the EU's revised Industrial Emissions Directive (IED) — the law setting pollution limits for large plants — leaving roughly 13,000 German facilities facing fixed new duties but no clarity on national rules or start dates. At the same time Berlin was shown to have lobbied to weaken the EU corporate supply-chain due-diligence law, a deregulatory pull in the opposite direction. A separate EU procedure (a "CLH" harmonised classification) could label talc — a common filler and additive in paints and coatings — as "presumed carcinogenic" and harmful to the lungs, which industry bodies including the German paints association VdL are contesting. Trade defences also spread: the UK will launch a carbon border tax (CBAM) on 1 January 2027 on imports such as fertiliser, and China renewed anti-dumping duties on copolymer polyoxymethylene (POM, an engineering plastic) from the US, EU, Japan and Taiwan.

Industry Impact

The signal for Henkel and peers is regulatory uncertainty on top of rising cost. The IED limbo makes plant-investment planning harder in Europe's largest chemical market, while a talc reclassification could force reformulation of many filled coatings and add labelling and handling costs. A UK carbon border tax raises the landed price of carbon-intensive inputs and invites retaliation — BRICS ministers this week branded CBAM an unfair trade barrier — and China's renewed POM duties keep engineering-plastic trade fragmented. Firms that track these overlapping rules early, and can certify low-carbon and reformulated products, turn the churn into an edge over slower rivals.

Frankfurter Allgemeine Zeitung | European Coatings | Frankfurter Rundschau | Yahoo | China Economic Net

item.title: Hours before the paused 50% US tariffs were due, the US–Canada deal took shape: duties on Canadian cars would fall to 15% and on steel and aluminium to 25%, Trump floated reviving the Keystone XL oil pipeline, and the deadline moved to Saturday.
item.description:
The last-minute reprieve reported yesterday firmed into concrete terms. Negotiators met for a third straight day, and sources described a deal that would cut the top tariff on Canadian-built cars and trucks from 25% to 15%, and halve metals duties to 25% — the lower steel rate applying only within a quota of about 4 million tonnes a year, with higher rates above it. In return Canada would drop retaliatory auto tariffs, ease dairy supply-management rules, and restore US alcohol and procurement access. Trump said Canada agreed to eliminate tariffs on US farm goods and, unexpectedly, suggested the cancelled Keystone XL cross-border oil pipeline "may be awoken from the grave" as part of the package. He pushed the 50% tariff start — on about USD 20 billion of goods, imposed under Section 338, a 1930s law allowing duties on countries judged to discriminate against US commerce — to Saturday 22 August. Separately, Mexico weighed tougher anti-dumping curbs on Chinese goods while pursuing its own USMCA extension.

Industry Impact

For construction-linked chemistries the détente is positive: cement, lumber, steel and aluminium sit at the base of building demand that drives sealants, adhesives and coatings, and a 15% auto rate would ease pressure on a major coatings-and-adhesives end-market. But the relief is provisional — a deadline extension, not a signed treaty — and the reach for a 1930s law shows the US will keep tariffs alive on several legal bases. Mexico's parallel move to raise anti-dumping walls against China signals North America hardening as a bloc, which reshapes where materials can be sourced tariff-free.

The Globe and Mail | MarketScreener | CBC | BBC News | South China Morning Post

item.title: With the US–Iran ceasefire lapsed, Trump threatened the "most crushing economic operation ever" against Iran and any country that helps it, the UAE halted all trade with Tehran after a missile hit its waters, and oil held above USD 90 a barrel.
item.description:
The nearly six-month war shifted further from diplomacy toward economic siege. President Trump said Iran had missed its chance for a deal and would face "economic warfare and isolation on an unprecedented scale", threatening "tremendous" punishment on any country, bank, company or airport that gives Iran a "lifeline" — a secondary-sanctions threat aimed at third countries, many of them Chinese. He added that no talks are scheduled. The pressure widened regionally: the United Arab Emirates, long one of Iran's main trade routes, announced an indefinite embargo on all trade and financial dealings with Iran after two ballistic missiles struck its waters (Iran denied responsibility, calling it a "false flag"). Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz — the channel for a fifth of the world's oil — stayed heavily disrupted, and Saudi Arabia resumed covert "dark voyage" ship-to-ship transfers off Oman after Houthis blockaded its Red Sea port of Yanbu. Brent held near USD 92, rising for a fourth straight day.

Industry Impact

A move from "seek a deal" to "strangle the economy" signals the oil-price premium and shipping disruption will persist, keeping crude-derived feedstocks — naphtha, solvents and many adhesive and coating raw materials — expensive and volatile, and lengthening Gulf shipping routes and lead times. The secondary-sanctions threat is the bigger new risk for manufacturers: any supplier, bank or logistics partner touching Iran-linked trade could be caught, so compliance teams should re-screen counterparties now. Higher energy costs also lift coal demand and power prices, feeding through to energy-intensive chemical production across Europe and Asia.

Al Jazeera | The Straits Times | Al Jazeera | The Times of India | Cnyes.com
